sections.topic: The definite article Al — ال التَّعْرِيف
sections.note: 1. ال = Al is the definite article in Arabic as The in English, e.g. يُوم = day, الْيُوم = the day (today) (Pronounciation: elyōm); تُوت = strawberry, التُّوت = the strawberry (Pronounciation: et-tūt). 2. Al is not always fully pronounced: it can be Al, El, Li or just A or E, e.g. التوت et-tūt. When Al is followed by a word starting with ت (as in توت), the ل of ال is not pronounced and instead the ت is doubled; the sign Shadda ( ّ ) indicates this doubling and appears above the letter: التّوت. If التّوت appears in the middle of a sentence, the ال is not pronounced at all and only the doubling of the ت indicates the definite article. 3. Out of the 28 Arabic letters, 14 letters cause the ل of ال to not be pronounced; they are called Sun letters (أَحْرُف شَمْسيّة). The rest are called Moon letters (أَحْرُف قَمَرية). We have learned so fur [sic] 3 sun letters: ت، ل، ن.

sections.topic: Introduction to roots and patterns
sections.note: Arabic verbs (and words in general) are a combination of a root and a pattern. The root usually consists of 3 consonants, and the pattern is a template for adding consonants and/or vowels (as prefixes, affixes and/or suffixes) to the root letters. Each root is used in more than one pattern, and each pattern is used for more than one root. The combination of root and pattern is what gives a word its specific semantic meaning. Example: the root و.ل.د combined with the pattern x-x́-x (fatha on 1st and 2nd radicals) forms وَلَد 'boy'; the same root in the pattern x-x-'alif-x́ gives a word with a different meaning: وَالِد 'parent'.

sections.topic: The conjugation of verbs in the perfect form (singular only)
sections.note: The simplest form of a verb is the 3rd person masculine singular of the perfect. For this person in the simple trilateral verb (a verb with a root of three radicals), the first and the third radicals are vocalized with a fatha. The second radical may be vocalized with a fatha (most common), kasra or (rarely) damma. The perfect form is conjugated by adding endings to the radicals of the verb (table: person / example / ending).

sections.topic: Word order in verbal sentences
sections.note: 1. If the subject of the sentence is an independent pronoun (I, he, she, etc.) and the predicate is a verb, the verb will follow its subject. 2. If the subject of the sentence is a noun and the predicate is a verb, the verb will usually precede its subject and agree with it in gender. (Footnote: It is allowed to place the verb after its subject in order to emphasize the subject or as a stylistic device. This word order is common in headlines of newspapers: أَلْوَزِير زَارَ لُبْنَان - the minister visited Lebanon.) 3. In a sentence that includes more than one verb, the first verb will precede its subject, and the other verbs will follow it.

sections.topic: The letters ظ and ض — أَحْرُف الظاء والضاد
sections.note: In MSA (Modern Standard Arabic) the letter ظ is pronounced as an emphatic /dh/ or /th/ (as in 'mother') whereas the letter ض is pronounced as an emphatic /d/. Arabic dialects however do not follow this pronunciation. The Arab world is divided into two dialect groups: the urban dialect, in which both ض and ظ are pronounced ض, and the rural dialect in which both ض and ظ are pronounced ظ. An exception to this rule is a group of words adopted from the MSA in which ظ is pronounced as an emphatic /z/.

sections.topic: The direct object pronouns (Pages 97-99)
sections.note: The direct object pronoun is attached to a verb and functions as its direct object. The direct object pronouns are identical to the possessive pronouns that are attached to nouns and prepositions, except for the pronoun of the 1st sing.: نِي. For example: he visited me - زَارَنِي (versus: my pen - قَلَمِي). Remarks: 1. In the form of the perfect verb in the 3rd person masc. pl. (they), the final 'alif (ـُوا) drops before adding the direct object pronoun. 2. The form of the perfect verb in the 2nd person masc. pl. before a direct object pronoun ends with tumū. 3. 'Alif maqṣūra (ى) at the end of a verb is changed to 'alif (ا) before a direct object pronoun. 4. The pronouns هُ ، هُمْ ، هُنَّ become هِ ، هِمْ ، هِنَّ after the perfect form of the 2nd fem. sg. (you).

sections.topic: The imperfect form
sections.note: 1. The imperfect is formed by adding prefixes to the radicals of the root of the verb. 2. The prefixes of the imperfect are: 'alif - I; nūn - we; tā' - you, she; yā' - he, they. The prefixes of the imperfect in the first form are vocalized with a fatḥa in all persons. 3. The first radical of the root is vocalized with a sukūn. 4. The second radical of the root is vocalized with a ḍamma, fatḥa or kasra, according to the pattern of the verb: يَدْرُسُ ، يَشْرَبُ ، يَنْزِلُ. 5. In persons that end with the third radical of the root - I, you (masc. sg.), he, she, we - the third radical is vocalized with a ḍamma. In the other forms, the vowel of the third radical changes according to the endings: you (fem. sg.) - ـِينَ; you (masc. pl.), they (masc.) - ـُونَ; you (fem. pl.), they (fem.) - ـْنَ

sections.topic: Remarks on the imperfect
sections.note: 1. Sometimes the vowel of the second radical of the imperfect can be predicted according to the pattern of the verb in the perfect form: a. If the verb in the perfect has the pattern fa'ala - ḍamma, kasra or fatḥa are possible. b. If the verb in the perfect has the pattern fa'ila - fatḥa. c. If the verb in the perfect has the pattern fa'ula - ḍamma. A rule of thumb: if the second or third radical of the root is one of the guttural consonants hamza (ء), hā' (ه), ḥā' (ح) or 'ayn (ع) - usually fatḥa - BUT not always. In this book and in several dictionaries the vowel of the second radical of the imperfect is indicated after the verb in the perfect: دَرَسَ ـُ ، ذَهَبَ ـَ ، نَزَلَ ـِ. 2. The imperfect in Arabic is usually used to denote an action in the present or in the future. 3. In order to explicitly indicate the future, the particle sawfa (سَوْفَ - independent word) or the prefix sa (سَـ - joins the verb) precede the imperfect verb. 4. To negate the imperfect the particle lā is used.

sections.topic: The case endings - 'al-'i'rāb - of definite nouns (Pages 140-143)
sections.note: The last consonant of nouns in Arabic is vocalized according to the grammatical function of the word in the sentence (subject, nominal predicate, direct object, adverb denoting time or place etc.). There are three cases in Arabic: nominative (raf'), accusative (naṣb) and genitive (jarr). A definite noun - either by a definite article, a possessive pronoun or by being the first element of a construct state - is vocalized with a ḍamma in the nominative case, a fatḥa in the accusative case, and a kasra in the genitive case. Nominative - the case of subjects and nominal predicates. Accusative - the case of direct objects and adverbs. Genitive - the case of nouns following a preposition and nouns which function as a second element in a construct state.

sections.topic: The Imperative ('al-'amr) of the first form (textbook pages 161-162)
sections.note: Remarks: 1. The imperative is used only for the 2nd person (you). 2. The imperative is derived from the imperfect of the 2nd person by omitting the prefixes: تَكْتُبُ ← أُكْتُبْ. 3. The vowels of the first and the second radicals of the root are identical to their equivalent vowels in the imperfect. 4. The third radical of the root is vocalized with a sukūn in the imperative of the 2nd masc. sg. and the 2nd fem. pl. The ending of the 2nd fem. sg. is: ـِي , and the ending of the 2nd masc. pl. is: ـُوا. 5. After the omission of the prefixes of the imperfect, the imperative form begins with a sukūn. Since words in Arabic cannot begin with a sukūn, an 'alif is prefixed to the imperative. This 'alif is vocalized with a ḍamma if the second radical of the imperative is vocalized with a ḍamma (أُكْتُبْ), and with a kasra if the second radical is vocalized either with a fatḥa or a kasra (إِجْلِسْ ، إِشْرَبْ). If the imperative does not introduce the sentence, this 'alif is not pronounced and is marked with a waṣla (like the 'alif of the definite article). For example: drink and go! إِشْرَبْ وَاذْهَبْا ('išrab waḏhab).

sections.topic: Imperative — additional remarks (hamza-initial and waw-initial verbs)
sections.note: Additional remarks: 1. The first radical - 'alif - of the verbs أَخَذَ 'to take', أَكَلَ 'to eat', and أَمَرَ 'to command', is omitted in the imperative: خُذْ - take!, كُلْ - eat!, مُرْ - command!. The rest of the conjugation is according to the rules and suffixes mentioned above, e.g.: خُذْ - take (masc. sg.)!, خُذِي - take (fem. sg.)!, خُذُوا - take (masc. pl.)!, خُذْنَ - take (fem. pl.)!. 2. Verbs with a wāw as their first radical are conjugated regularly in the perfect, whereas in the imperfect and the imperative the wāw is omitted.

sentences.ar: يندمج التعليم في الجامعة المفتوحة مع مسار حياتك الديناميكي: أثناء الدراسة في المرحلة الثانويّة، أو أثناء حياتك المهنيّة أو بموازاة تطوير شركة أو مشروع ناشئ (ستارت أب).

الجامعة المفتوحة هي أكبر جامعة في البلاد: يدرس فيها أكثر من 46,000 طالبًا وطالبة (من بينهم 7000 من الطلّاب العرب)، ويتخرّج منها حوالي 4,000 من الخرّيجين الجدد في كلّ عام (من بينهم مئات الخرّيجين من العرب).
لدراسة للقب الأوّل واللقب الثاني في مجالات عديدة ومتنوّعة.
المرونة الكبيرة في اختيار طريقة التعليم: التدريس الوجاهي (وجهًا لوجه) في صفوف صغيرة مع استخدام تكنولوجيا التعليم المتطورة.
"بداية سهلة": إمكانيّة الدراسة وإجراء الامتحانات باللغة العربيّة في المساقات (الدورات) التعليميّة الأولى، الاستشارة والإرشاد باللغة العربيّة، وورش عمل للتجسير باللغة العبريّة والإنجليزيّة.
المرافقة والمتابعة الأكاديميّة على مدى فترة الدراسة.
